sheet.howExamined: B2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. DNA usually appears in the last third of the paper, worth about 6 to 11 marks across a question, opened by a drawing of the molecule: which part is the base [1], name the two substances of the backbone [2], then the base-percentage calculation [3] and, at Higher, the number of amino acids [1]. Summer 2025 ran it as B2 Higher Q10; Summer 2023 asked Foundation candidates for the shape of the molecule and where DNA is found (Q3).
traps: Naming only one of the two backbone substances: in Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q10 most candidates could name one. Learn phosphate and deoxyribose as a pair

The base-percentage chain: in Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q10 quite a few candidates calculated it correctly, and each line carries a mark: double the given base, take that from 100, then halve what is left

Counting the amino acids a length of DNA codes for: Summer 2025 B2 Higher Q10 found it difficult for many. Three bases in a row on one strand code for one amino acid, so count the bases along one strand and divide by three
Not giving the exact name for the shape: in Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q3 only quite a few candidates wrote double helix
Chromosome numbers in cells other than body cells: Summer 2023 B2 Foundation Q3 records a surprising lack of knowledge of the number in an egg cell and a fertilised egg
Defining the genome: Summer 2024 B2 Higher Q10 notes that the mark went to candidates who had learned the definition, all the genetic material of an organism
Naming the idea that three bases code for one amino acid: many gave base triplet in Summer 2023 B2 Higher Q10; CCEA's schemes refuse 'triple base' and 'triplet base'
The word genome inside a genetic engineering question: only the better candidates gave it in Summer 2023 B2 Higher Q7(a)

noteBlocks.md: As in the drawing, the same instructions have names at four sizes. The **genome** is all of an organism's genetic material. A **chromosome** is one long thread of DNA in the nucleus. A **gene** is a short length of DNA on a chromosome that controls a characteristic, by coding for a protein.

noteBlocks.md: An **allele** is a different form of the same gene: fur length in rabbits is the gene, and its long and short versions are alleles. A chromosome is *made of* DNA, as a book is made of paper; a gene is one sentence in it, not the whole book.

noteBlocks.stem: A tomato plant has a length of DNA that controls fruit colour; one form of it gives red fruit and another gives yellow. Name each of these. (a) All of the tomato plant's genetic material. (b) The length of DNA for fruit colour. (c) The red-fruit form of that length. [3]

steps.working: (a) The genome.
steps.decision: All of an organism's genetic material, every chromosome together, is its genome.

steps.working: (b) A gene.
steps.decision: One short length of DNA controlling one characteristic, here fruit colour.

steps.working: (c) An allele.
steps.decision: A different form of that same gene: red is one form, yellow another.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these is a genome?
options: all the DNA in one oak tree
the DNA that controls leaf shape in an oak
the round-leaf form of that DNA
noteBlocks.answer: all the DNA in one oak tree
noteBlocks.explain: Sort by size, as the worked answer did: the genome is all of the genetic material, a gene is one length of it, and an allele is one form of a gene. Only 'all the DNA in one oak tree' is everything, so that is the genome.

optionNotes.option: the DNA that controls leaf shape in an oak
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is real genetic material, but one length of DNA controlling one characteristic is a gene, not the whole genome.

optionNotes.option: the round-leaf form of that DNA
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is about the oak's DNA too, but one form of a gene is an allele, the smallest of the words.

twin.prompt: Which of these is an allele?
options: the wrinkled-seed form of the pea seed-shape gene
all the DNA in one pea plant
the whole length of DNA for seed shape
twin.answer: the wrinkled-seed form of the pea seed-shape gene
twin.explain: An allele is one form of a gene: wrinkled is one form of the seed-shape gene. All the DNA is the genome, and the whole length for seed shape is the gene.

optionNotes.option: all the DNA in one pea plant
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is the pea plant's genetic material, but all of it together is the genome, the largest of the four words.

optionNotes.option: the whole length of DNA for seed shape
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is about seed shape, but the whole length for one characteristic is the gene; an allele is one form of it.

noteBlocks.caption: Real chromosomes, cut out and sorted into pairs. Count the pairs, not the chromosomes.
noteBlocks.prompt: How many pairs can you count, and what is different about the pair at the bottom right?

noteBlocks.md: In a body cell the chromosomes sit in **functional pairs**, one of each pair from each parent: 23 pairs in a human body cell. A **gamete**, a sperm cell or an egg cell, carries one chromosome of each pair, so it has half the number.
Bacteria break the rule another way: a bacterium has **no nucleus**, just one loop of DNA and a few small rings called plasmids, so its chromosomes are not in pairs.

noteBlocks.stem: A mouse's body cells each hold 40 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in the nucleus of (a) a mouse egg cell and (b) a fertilised mouse egg? [2]

steps.decision: An egg cell is a gamete: it carries one chromosome from each pair, so half the body cell's number.
Fertilisation joins the egg's set to the sperm's set, so the fertilised egg has the full number again, in pairs.

noteBlocks.prompt: A goat's body cells each hold 60 chromosomes. How many functional pairs is that?
noteBlocks.explain: Chromosomes in a body cell come in pairs, two to a pair, as the worked answer used: 60 ÷ 2 = 30 pairs. That is also the number a goat's gamete holds.

twin.prompt: A horse's body cells hold 32 pairs of chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a horse's sperm cell?
twin.explain: A sperm cell carries one chromosome from each pair, so it holds 32.

noteBlocks.md: Unwind a chromosome far enough and you reach **DNA**. Each backbone is a chain of **phosphate** and **sugar (deoxyribose)**, in turn. A **base** sticks out from each sugar, and the bases pair across the middle: **A with T**, **C with G**. The two backbones twist round each other: a **double helix**.

noteBlocks.title: Why A only pairs with T
noteBlocks.md: A and G are large bases; T and C are small. A large base always pairs with a small one, so every rung is the same length and the backbones stay parallel. A joins T by two bonds, C joins G by three, so A never fits C.

noteBlocks.stem: A student builds a model of DNA from sweets and cocktail sticks. Describe what the finished model must show. [3]

steps.working: Two backbones, each a chain of phosphate and sugar (deoxyribose) pieces in turn.
steps.decision: Start with the backbone and name both of its substances: one alone earns only half of it.

steps.working: Bases joined across between the backbones in pairs: A with T, and C with G.
steps.decision: Then the rungs, with the pairing rules, which never change.

steps.working: The whole ladder twisted into a double helix.
steps.decision: Then the shape, by its name.

noteBlocks.title: GCSE Biology Revision "DNA and the Genome"
noteBlocks.why: A second voice on the four words, with the double helix drawn as you watch.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the model, which base must sit opposite every thymine (T)?
options: adenine (A)
cytosine (C)
guanine (G)
noteBlocks.explain: The pairing rules never change, as step 2 of the worked answer said: A with T, C with G. So every T in the model has an A opposite it, a large base with a small one.

optionNotes.option: cytosine (C)
optionNotes.why: It tempts because C and T are both small bases, but two small bases would make a short rung, and C pairs only with G.

optionNotes.option: guanine (G)
optionNotes.why: It tempts because T is small and needs a large partner, but of the two large bases only A fits T's two bonds; G pairs with C, by three.

twin.prompt: In the model, which base must sit opposite every cytosine (C)?
options: guanine (G)
adenine (A)
thymine (T)
twin.explain: C always pairs with G. A pairs with T.

optionNotes.option: adenine (A)
optionNotes.why: It tempts because A is a large base, as C needs, but A pairs only with T, by two bonds, and C needs a partner with three.

optionNotes.option: thymine (T)
optionNotes.why: It tempts because T is the other small base, but two small bases would make a short rung, and T pairs only with A.

noteBlocks.md: Because the pairing rules never change, one strand tells you the other. Work along it one base at a time: every A gives a T, every T an A, every C a G and every G a C. Write the two rules in the margin first, and check the new strand is the same length.
The rules give you the partner of every base, but nothing fixes the order along a strand. That order, the **base sequence**, differs between people: only identical twins share one.

noteBlocks.stem: One strand of DNA reads C A T T G C. Write the sequence of bases on the other strand. [2]

steps.working: C → G, A → T, T → A
steps.decision: One base at a time, left to right, using the two rules.

steps.working: T → A, G → C, C → G, so the strand reads G T A A C G
steps.decision: Finish the run and count: six bases in, six bases out.

noteBlocks.prompt: One strand of DNA reads T T G A. Which strand pairs with it?
options: A A C T
T T G A
A A G T
noteBlocks.explain: Swap each base for its partner, as the worked answer did: T gives A, T gives A, G gives C and A gives T. So the paired strand is A A C T.

optionNotes.option: T T G A
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is the strand you were given, but the opposite strand holds each base's partner, not the same base.

optionNotes.option: A A G T
optionNotes.why: It tempts because the T bases became A correctly, but G pairs with C, not G, and A pairs with T.

twin.prompt: One strand of DNA reads G C C A. Which strand pairs with it?
options: C G G T
G C C A
C G G A
twin.explain: G gives C, C gives G, C gives G and A gives T: C G G T.

optionNotes.option: G C C A
optionNotes.why: It tempts because it is the strand you were given, but the paired strand holds each base's partner, not the same base.

optionNotes.option: C G G A
optionNotes.why: It tempts because its first three bases are right, but the last A pairs with T, not with another A.

noteBlocks.caption: Each triplet of three bases codes for one amino acid, so 12 bases code for a chain of 4.

noteBlocks.md: The order of the bases is a code, read **three at a time** along one strand. Each group of three, a **base triplet**, codes for one **amino acid**; the amino acids join in that order to make a protein. This is the **base triplet hypothesis**.
A double strand is counted along one strand only: its number of base pairs is the number of bases to divide by three.

noteBlocks.stem:
(a) One strand of a gene carries 30 bases. How many amino acids does it code for? [1]
(b) A double strand of DNA has 27 base pairs. How many amino acids does it code for? [1]

steps.working: (a) 30 ÷ 3 = 10 amino acids
steps.decision: Three bases make one triplet, and one triplet codes for one amino acid.

steps.working: (b) 27 base pairs means 27 bases along one strand: 27 ÷ 3 = 9
steps.decision: Only one strand is read, so count the pairs, not both strands' bases.

noteBlocks.prompt: A double strand of DNA has 48 base pairs. How many amino acids does it code for?
noteBlocks.explain: Read along one strand, as the worked answer did for its base pairs: 48 pairs is 48 bases on that strand, and 48 ÷ 3 = 16. Counting both strands gives 32, twice too many.

twin.prompt: One strand carries 36 bases. How many amino acids does it code for?
twin.explain: 36 ÷ 3 = 12: one amino acid for every three bases.

noteBlocks.text: Higher: reading the code with a table

noteBlocks.md: A question gives a table of base triplets and the amino acid each codes for. Read the strand three at a time and look each triplet up. A **mutation** changes a base: the new triplet may code for a different amino acid, which can change the protein's shape so it no longer works, or for the same one, so nothing changes.

noteBlocks.stem:
Use the table. One strand reads TGT GGA AAA.
(a) Name the three amino acids in order. [2]
(b) A mutation changes the last triplet from AAA to AAG. What happens to the protein? [1]

data.caption: Part of a table of base triplets on the coding strand

steps.working: TGT codes for cysteine, and GGA for glycine.
steps.decision: Split the strand into triplets first, then look each one up in turn.

steps.working: AAA codes for lysine, so the order is cysteine, glycine, lysine.
steps.decision: Keep the order of the triplets: it is the order of the amino acids in the protein.

steps.working: AAG also codes for lysine, so the protein does not change.
steps.decision: Look the new triplet up too: a base change does not always change the amino acid.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the table, AAA codes for lysine and GAA for glutamate. A mutation changes AAA to GAA. What is the effect?
options: lysine is replaced by glutamate, so the protein may change
nothing changes, because only one base changed
the protein loses an amino acid
noteBlocks.answer: lysine is replaced by glutamate, so the protein may change
noteBlocks.explain: Look the new triplet up, as step 3 of the worked answer did. This time GAA codes for a different amino acid, so one amino acid in the chain changes, and the protein's shape, and so its job, may change with it.

optionNotes.option: nothing changes, because only one base changed
optionNotes.why: It tempts because one base seems a small change, but look the new triplet up: GAA codes for a different amino acid.

optionNotes.option: the protein loses an amino acid
optionNotes.why: It tempts because a mutation sounds like damage, but the triplet is still three bases, so it still codes for one amino acid, a different one.

twin.prompt: In the table, GGA and GGC both code for glycine. A mutation changes GGA to GGC. What is the effect?
options: no change: it still codes for glycine
glycine is replaced by a different amino acid
the protein gains an amino acid
twin.answer: no change: it still codes for glycine
twin.explain: GGC codes for glycine too, so the same amino acid is used and the protein does not change.

optionNotes.option: glycine is replaced by a different amino acid
optionNotes.why: It tempts because a base did change, but the table gives GGC as glycine too, so the amino acid stays the same.

optionNotes.option: the protein gains an amino acid
optionNotes.why: It tempts because a mutation sounds like a change in size, but one base is swapped for another, so the number of triplets stays the same.

noteBlocks.md: **A drawing first.** Which lettered part is the base, then name both backbone substances, phosphate and sugar (deoxyribose): in Summer 2025 most named one of the two, and fewer named both.
**The percentage chain.** A base's percentage, the pair doubled, taken from 100 and halved, with each step on its own line (Summer 2019, Summer 2025).
**The genome inside another topic.** Genetic engineering questions ask what the genome is: all of an organism's genetic material (Summer 2023, Summer 2024).

noteBlocks.stem: A human insulin gene is put into a bacterium's DNA. Explain whether the bacterium's genome has changed. [2]

steps.working: The genome is all of an organism's genetic material.
steps.decision: Start from the definition, the mark examiners give to candidates who learned it.

steps.working: The bacterium's genetic material now includes the human gene, so its genome has changed.
steps.decision: Then apply it: anything added to the DNA is part of the genome.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these changes a plant's genome?
options: adding a gene from a bacterium to its DNA
cutting off one of its leaves
growing it in brighter light
noteBlocks.answer: adding a gene from a bacterium to its DNA
noteBlocks.explain: The genome is all of the genetic material, as step 1 of the worked answer said, so only a change to the DNA changes it. Adding a gene does; losing a leaf or growing in brighter light leaves the DNA of every cell as it was.

optionNotes.option: cutting off one of its leaves
optionNotes.why: It tempts because the plant has lost part of itself, but every remaining cell still holds the same genetic material.

optionNotes.option: growing it in brighter light
optionNotes.why: It tempts because light changes how the plant grows, but that is the environment acting, and its DNA stays the same.

twin.prompt: Which of these is part of a bacterium's genome?
options: the genes on its plasmids
the sugar it uses for respiration
the wall around the cell
twin.explain: A bacterium's genetic material is its loop of DNA and its plasmids, so plasmid genes are part of its genome. Sugar and the cell wall are not genetic material.

optionNotes.option: the sugar it uses for respiration
optionNotes.why: It tempts because the sugar is inside the bacterium, but it is fuel for respiration, not genetic material.

optionNotes.option: the wall around the cell
optionNotes.why: It tempts because the wall is part of the bacterium, but it is not made of DNA, so it is not part of the genome.

options.feedback: All of it: every chromosome, every gene, every base.

items.stem: How many chromosomes are there in the nucleus of a human body cell?

options.feedback: 23 pairs, two in each pair, so 46.

options.text: it is different in every person

parts.workedSolution: T pairs with A, so A is 36% as well: 36 + 36 = 72%. That leaves 100 − 72 = 28% for C and G together, and they are equal, so C is 28 ÷ 2 = 14%.

The halving comes at the end, and it is what is LEFT that gets halved, not the percentage you were given.

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: Two losses to watch for. The first is a gene and an allele given the same definition, which costs a whole indicative point however well the rest is written. The second is the shape: only the words double helix earn that point, and 'spiral' or 'twisted ladder' does not. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Go outward from the smallest thing: bases, DNA, gene, chromosome, genome.
Give an example of an allele so that the difference from a gene is visible.
parts.workedSolution: A DNA molecule is built from two long strands. Each strand has a backbone made of a phosphate and a sugar, deoxyribose, repeating along its length, and the bases stick out from that backbone. The bases interlink across the middle in a fixed way: A always pairs with T, and C always pairs with G. The two strands twist around each other to form a double helix. A chromosome is one long thread of this DNA, held in the nucleus, and in a human body cell the chromosomes lie in functional pairs, 23 pairs in all. A gene is a short length of DNA on a chromosome that controls a characteristic, such as flower colour. An allele is a different form of the same gene, such as the allele for violet flowers and the allele for white flowers. Taken together, all of the genetic material of the organism is its genome.

commonErrors.feedback: A gene and an allele have been given the same definition. The gene is the place and the job; the allele is the version sitting there.

parts.stem:
The diagram shows two rungs of a DNA molecule. The bases are drawn to show their relative sizes, and each short line between two bases is one bond.
Base W is guanine (G). Name base X.

accepted: cytosine

hints: Which base always pairs with G?
parts.workedSolution: Cytosine (C): guanine always pairs with cytosine.

parts.stem: Base Z is adenine (A). Working from the drawing alone, suggest two reasons why W bonds with X but never with Z.

accepted: A large base must pair with a small base, and W and Z are both large; the paired bases must have the same number of bonds, and W has three while Z has two.

scheme.for: a large base pairs with a small base (W and Z are both large, so the rung would be too long)
paired bases have the same number of bonds (W has three, Z two)

hints: Compare the widths of the bases.
Count the short lines on each rung.
parts.workedSolution: A large base always pairs with a small one, so every rung is the same length: W and Z are both large. Paired bases must also have the same number of bonds: W makes three, Z only two.

findTheMistake.stem:
Ciara is asked: 'In a length of DNA, 28% of the bases are A. Calculate the percentage of the bases that are C. [3]'
Her working:
studentWorking: A pairs with T, so T is 28% as well
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are exactly right, and they carry two of the three marks. Line 3 hands the whole of the remaining 44% to C. But C pairs with G, so those two must be equal and the 44% is shared between them.
correction: A pairs with T, so T is 28% as well
findTheMistake.feedback: Two marks of the three. A quick check catches the rest: add her four percentages up and you get 144, not 100.

findTheMistake.stem:
Oisín is asked: 'A double strand of DNA has 21 base pairs. How many amino acids does it code for? [1]'
His working:
studentWorking: 21 base pairs is 42 bases in all
so it codes for 14 amino acids
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The code is read along one strand only. 21 base pairs means 21 bases on that strand, so line 1 doubles the count, and lines 2 and 3 carry the error on. Summer 2025 examiners found this count difficult for many.
correction: 21 base pairs is 21 bases along one strand
so it codes for 7 amino acids
findTheMistake.feedback: No mark as written: the answer is 7. Divide the number of base pairs by three, never the bases of both strands.

prompts.answer: Divide by three, because a base triplet of three bases codes for one amino acid.

prompts.answer: 20%, because every A pairs with a T.
